name: wide_f64_add_relu2
targeted_gap: TILE_BYTES=8192 byte budget is dtype-blind: for float64 (itemsize 8) it shrinks the seed tile to ~256 elems, 1/4 of the default's 1024, so the seed under-fills each program vs the compiler default [32,32].
hypothesis: bytes_per_elem = 3 loads/stores * 8 = 24, so budget_target = 8192//24 = 341 -> pow2 256. Fully-tiled 2D f64: seed distributes inner-first to [1,256] (wide-N) or [2,128] (mod-N) = 256 elems/program, while the default [32,32] holds 1024 elems. The wide-dtype budget starves the tile: 4x fewer elements per program => 4x more tiny programs, worse launch/scheduling amortization on a bandwidth-bound kernel. The mod-N [8192,128] shape (seed [2,128], only 2 rows) is the sharpest: default's [32,32] has 16x the rows per program.

name: wide_f64_rope_rotate
targeted_gap: The register cap (REGISTER_BYTES=65536) OVER-collapses the partial-tiling tile for float64: it was calibrated on fp32 compute (compute_itemsize=4), but float64's compute_itemsize=8 doubles the counted reg pressure, driving reg_cap and budget_target to 1 even for a MODERATE heads*head_dim slab -> the seed tiles the outer dims to [1,1], one slab per program, launching a huge grid of tiny programs vs the default [B,32].
hypothesis: RoPE-mimic (tile [batch,seq], flow the full [heads,head_dim] float64 slab through reshape/split/join as elementwise so pointwise fires). slab = heads*head_dim; bytes_per_elem = 3*slab*8. For H=4,D=64 slab=256 => bpe=6144 => budget_target=1, reg_cap=10 -> target=1 -> seed [1,1]. Each program processes ONE (batch,seq) point but drags the whole heads*head_dim slab; grid = batch*seq programs. The default [8,32]=256 outer points/program does 256x fewer, better-occupied launches. This is the RoPE failure class recurring through a wide dtype -- the reg-cap fix over-corrects and starves occupancy instead of the old over-tiling overflow.

@helion.kernel()
def wide_f64_rope_rotate(x, cos, sin):
    batch, heads, seq_len, head_dim = x.size()
    half = head_dim // 2
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    for tb, tt in hl.tile([batch, seq_len]):
        cos_pair = (
            cos[tb, tt, :]
            .to(torch.float32)
            .reshape([tb, tt, 2, half])
            .permute(0, 1, 3, 2)
        )
        sin_pair = (
            sin[tb, tt, :]
            .to(torch.float32)
            .reshape([tb, tt, 2, half])
            .permute(0, 1, 3, 2)
        )
        cos_first, cos_second = hl.split(cos_pair)
        sin_first, sin_second = hl.split(sin_pair)
        x_pair = (
            x[tb, :, tt, :]
            .to(torch.float32)
            .reshape([tb, heads, tt, 2, half])
            .permute(0, 1, 2, 4, 3)
        )
        x_first, x_second = hl.split(x_pair)
        x_first_out = x_first * cos_first[:, None, :, :] - x_second * sin_first[:, None, :, :]
        x_second_out = x_second * cos_second[:, None, :, :] + x_first * sin_second[:, None, :, :]
        out[tb, :, tt, :] = (
            hl.join(x_first_out, x_second_out)
            .permute(0, 1, 2, 4, 3)
            .reshape([tb, heads, tt, head_dim])
            .to(out.dtype)
        )
    return out


def make_inputs(shape):
    batch, heads, seq_len, head_dim = shape
    x = torch.randn(shape, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float64)
    angles = torch.randn([batch, seq_len, head_dim], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float64)
    cos = torch.cos(angles)
    sin = torch.sin(angles)
    return (x, cos, sin)

name: wide_f64_3d_fma
targeted_gap: For a 3-D fully-tiled float64 kernel the byte budget both shrinks the tile AND collapses the two outer block dims to 1: seed [1,1,256] (256 elems) vs the balanced default [16,16,16] (4096 elems), so the seed is 16x smaller and completely flat across two axes.
hypothesis: bytes_per_elem = 3*8 = 24 -> budget_target = 341 -> pow2 256, distributed innermost-first: inner absorbs 256 (>= floor), leftover budget 341//256 = 1 so both outer dims stay 1 => seed [1,1,256]. The 3-D default fragment gives [16,16,16] = 4096 elems (16x larger, balanced across all axes). The seed's [1,1,256] slice is a single 256-wide contiguous run per program with two axes pinned to 1: for a large 3-D f64 tensor this launches 16x more programs each moving a thin slab, starving occupancy/bandwidth vs the cubic default tile. Wide dtype makes the byte budget bite harder than it does for bf16 (where budget_target ~1365 would fill the inner and still spill to the outer).
